## Setup

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

load(url(
  "https://github.com/GarciaRios/govt_3990/raw/gh-pages/Labs/lab6/acs.RData"
))

acs_emp <- acs |>
  filter(
    employment == "employed",
    income > 0,
    !is.na(hrs_work)
  )
```

# Exercises

## Exercise 1: Scatterplot

```{r}
ggplot(
  acs_emp,
  aes(x = hrs_work, y = income)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours worked per week",
    y = "Annual income ($)",
    title = "Annual income and weekly hours worked"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Describe the direction, form, strength, and unusual observations.

> 

Does a straight line seem like a useful summary?

> 

## Exercise 2: Correlation

```{r}
acs_emp |>
  summarise(
    r = cor(hrs_work, income)
  )
```

What is the correlation?

> 

Interpret its direction and strength.

> 

Does it match what you saw in the scatterplot?

> 

## Exercise 3: Add the regression line

```{r}
ggplot(
  acs_emp,
  aes(x = hrs_work, y = income)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours worked per week",
    y = "Annual income ($)",
    title = "Annual income and weekly hours worked",
    subtitle = "Simple linear regression line"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Does the direction of the fitted line agree with the correlation?

> 

What does the line summarize that the correlation coefficient alone does not?

> 

## Exercise 4: Fit the model

```{r}
income_hours_model <- lm(
  income ~ hrs_work,
  data = acs_emp
)

summary(income_hours_model)
```

Write the fitted regression equation.

> 

Interpret the slope.

> 

Interpret the intercept. Is it substantively meaningful?

> 

## Exercise 5: \(R^2\)

Report and interpret \(R^2\).

> 

Check the relationship between correlation and \(R^2\):

```{r}
r_hours_income <- cor(
  acs_emp$hrs_work,
  acs_emp$income
)

r_hours_income^2
```

Does \(r^2\) match the model's \(R^2\)?

> 

## Exercise 6: Prediction

```{r}
predict(
  income_hours_model,
  newdata = data.frame(
    hrs_work = 40
  )
)
```

What income does the model predict for someone working 40 hours per week?

> 

Compare several work-hour values:

```{r}
prediction_cases <- data.frame(
  hrs_work = c(20, 40, 60)
)

prediction_cases |>
  mutate(
    predicted_income = predict(
      income_hours_model,
      newdata = prediction_cases
    )
  )
```

How do the predictions change? Connect the change to the slope.

> 

Why are these predicted incomes rather than what a person will necessarily earn?

> 

## Exercise 7: Extrapolation

```{r}
range(acs_emp$hrs_work)
```

Why would it be risky to predict income for a number of weekly work hours far outside this range?

> 

## Exercise 8: Compare another predictor

```{r}
ggplot(
  acs_emp,
  aes(x = age, y = income)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Annual income ($)",
    title = "Annual income and age"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
acs_emp |>
  summarise(
    r = cor(age, income, use = "complete.obs")
  )
```

```{r}
income_age_model <- lm(
  income ~ age,
  data = acs_emp
)

summary(income_age_model)
```

Describe the relationship.

> 

What is the correlation?

> 

Write the fitted equation and interpret the slope.

> 

Report \(R^2\).

> 

Which variable accounts for more variation in income: `hrs_work` or `age`?

> 

Does a straight line seem equally appropriate for both relationships?

>
